title: Ang 862–869: Guru Arjan in Gond
tomorrow: what did the elephant do when it was driven at Kabir?

lines: THE GURU'S IMAGE, IN THE MIND.
cards: Packing to leave home has its own math: one suitcase, a whole life. Photos? The sweater that smells like the house?
On ang 864, Guru Arjan names one thing that fits in no suitcase, and says to carry it everywhere: the Guru's image, held in the mind.

teach.h: THE GURU'S IMAGE IN THE MIND.
teach.b: Guru Arjan's hymns fill these pages of Gond.

The one on ang 864, in paraphrase: meditate on the Guru's image in your mind; let your mind take the Guru's Word as its mantra. Keep the Guru's feet in your heart; bow always to the Guru, the Supreme Lord.
Then a warning: let no one in the world wander in doubt; without the Guru, no one crosses over. The word for image is murat. And here's the surprise.
In Sikh practice the Guru isn't a statue to keep on a shelf, and Sikh teachers read this image through the very next line: the Guru's Word, the shabad, is what the mind holds.

teach.h: AN IMAGE THAT TRAVELS AS WORDS.
teach.b: So the image travels as words.

teach.h: WHAT TO CARRY WHEN YOU GO.
teach.b: Learned, sung, remembered. It's why Sikhs honor the Granth itself as the Guru, at the center of a gurdwara, and why a hymn can go with someone into a dorm room, a truck cab, or a hospital hallway.
So the packing math changes. A family won't fit in a bag. But a line you know by heart takes no space at all.
Guru Arjan's Gond is a lesson in what to carry: the Word, held inside, bowed to, and taken along.

how: Sikhs honor the Guru Granth Sahib as the Guru; some keep a gutka, a small book of daily hymns, or know shabads by heart, carrying the Word with them away from home.

games.q: your friend is moving across the country and says she'll lose her faith without her family's gurdwara. by ang 864, what does she still have?
o: the Word she knows by heart, which goes wherever she goes.
nothing; faith only lives inside the building.
a picture of the Guru, which does the same job.
games.why: Guru Arjan places the Guru's image in the mind and the Word in it as the mantra: it travels.

practice: Pick one line you love, from the Granth, a hymn, or someone wise. Say it once slowly aloud, then once more without looking. For the sit, hold it the way you'd hold something packed carefully, right at the top.
If you'd like, read the hymn on ang 864 first.
